questions.q: Logic is the study of reasoning. In studying it, the emphasis is placed on which of the following?
o: The grammar and vocabulary of sentences
The factual accuracy of each individual statement
The relationship between statements rather than their subject matter
questions.e: Logic is the study of reasoning and focuses on the relationship between statements, not on their content or subject matter.

questions.q: A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false. Which of the following is NOT a proposition?
o: Ibrahim is wearing a red coat
Buy two tickets for the movie
questions.e: A proposition must be a declarative sentence with a definite truth value. 'Buy two tickets for the movie' is a command (imperative), so it is neither true nor false.

questions.q: What is the name of the area of logic that deals with propositions?
questions.e: The area of logic dealing with propositions is called propositional calculus (or propositional logic).

questions.q: The conjunction of two propositions p and q is denoted by which symbol?
questions.e: The conjunction 'p and q' is denoted p ∧ q; the disjunction 'p or q' is p ∨ q.

questions.q: The disjunction of two propositions p and q ('p or q') is denoted by which symbol?
questions.e: The disjunction 'p or q' is written p ∨ q; the wedge ∧ is used for conjunction ('and').

questions.q: Which of the following symbols is NOT used to represent the negation (contradictory) of a proposition A?
questions.e: Negation of A is written as ~A, ¬A, or 'not-A'. The symbol ∧ denotes conjunction, not negation.

questions.q: A conjunction p ∧ q is true in which case?
o: Only when both p and q are false
When at least one of p or q is true
Only when both p and q are true
When p and q have different truth values
questions.e: A conjunction is true only when both of its component propositions are true.

questions.q: A disjunction p ∨ q is false in which case?
o: Only when both p and q are true
Only when both p and q are false
When exactly one of p or q is true
questions.e: A disjunction is true whenever at least one component is true, so it is false only when both components are false.

questions.q: Let p be 'A decade is 10 years' (true) and q be 'A millennium is 100 years' (false). What is the truth value of the conjunction p ∧ q?
questions.e: A millennium is 1000 years, so q is false. A conjunction is true only when both parts are true; since q is false, p ∧ q is false.

questions.q: Let p be 'A decade is 10 years' (true) and q be 'A millennium is 100 years' (false). What is the truth value of the disjunction p ∨ q?
questions.e: A disjunction is true when at least one part is true. Since p is true, p ∨ q is true regardless of q.

questions.q: The contradictory (negation) 'not-A' always has which truth value relative to A?
o: The same truth value as A
The opposite truth value of A
questions.e: The contradictory not-A is defined to always have the opposite truth value of A: if A is true, not-A is false, and vice versa.

questions.q: A compound statement of the form 'A and B and C and D and E' is classified as which type of proposition?
questions.e: Joining propositions with 'and', even several of them, forms a conjunction and follows the same logical rules as 'A and B'.

questions.q: In propositional logic, words such as 'but', 'although', 'however', and 'yet' are treated as which connective?
questions.e: Words like 'but', 'although', 'however', and 'yet' join two propositions and function logically the same as 'and' (conjunction).

questions.q: How should 'There is a hurricane but it is not raining' be written symbolically, where p: 'There is a hurricane' and q: 'It is raining'?
questions.e: 'But' is a conjunction and 'not raining' is ¬q, so the statement is p ∧ ¬q.

questions.q: Given p is true, q is true, and r is false, what is the value of (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r?
Given p = false, q = true, and r = false, what is the value of ¬(p ∨ q) ∧ (¬p ∨ r)?
questions.e: (p ∨ q) = (F ∨ T) = T, so ¬(p ∨ q) = F. A conjunction with a false part is false, so the whole expression is false.

questions.q: Given p = false and q = true, what is the value of ¬p ∨ ¬q?
questions.e: ¬p = T and ¬q = F, so ¬p ∨ ¬q = T ∨ F = T.

questions.q: The negation of the true statement 'Benny Goodman recorded music' has which truth value, and how is it written symbolically (with p as the original statement)?
questions.e: Negating a true statement gives a false one, so its truth value is False, and it is written ~p (e.g. 'Benny Goodman did not record music').

questions.q: Let p: 'Today is Monday', q: 'It is raining outside', r: 'It is hot'. The symbolic form ¬p ∧ (q ∨ r) reads as:
o: If today is not Monday then it is raining or hot
Today is not Monday or it is raining outside and it is hot
Today is Monday and it is raining outside and it is hot
Today is not Monday and either it is raining outside or it is hot
questions.e: ¬p is 'Today is not Monday', joined by ∧ ('and') to the disjunction (q ∨ r), 'either it is raining outside or it is hot'.

questions.q: Suppose smartphone A has 256 MB RAM, smartphone B has 288 MB RAM, and smartphone C has 128 MB RAM. What is the truth value of 'Smartphone B has the most RAM of these three'?
questions.e: 288 MB (B) is greater than 256 MB (A) and 128 MB (C), so the statement that B has the most RAM is true.

questions.q: In the conditional proposition p → q ('if p then q'), what is p called?
questions.e: In p → q, p is the hypothesis or antecedent and q is the conclusion or consequent.

questions.q: In the conditional proposition p → q, what is q called?
questions.e: In p → q, q is the conclusion or consequent; p is the hypothesis or antecedent.

questions.q: A conditional proposition p → q is false in exactly which case?
o: When p is false and q is true
When both p and q are true
When both p and q are false
When p is true and q is false
questions.e: A conditional is false only when its hypothesis is true but its conclusion is false; in all other cases it is true.

questions.q: What is the converse of the conditional proposition p → q?
questions.e: The converse of p → q is q → p (the hypothesis and conclusion are swapped).

questions.q: What is the contrapositive of the conditional proposition p → q?
questions.e: The contrapositive (transposition) of p → q is ¬q → ¬p, and it is logically equivalent to the original conditional.

questions.q: What is the inverse of the conditional proposition p → q?
questions.e: The inverse of p → q is ¬p → ¬q (both parts negated, order unchanged).

questions.q: Which form is logically equivalent to the conditional proposition p → q?
questions.e: The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p is an alternative, logically equivalent form of the conditional. The converse and inverse are not equivalent to it.

questions.q: The biconditional 'p if and only if q' is denoted and read as:
questions.e: The biconditional is written p ↔ q and read 'p if and only if q' (abbreviated 'p iff q').

questions.q: A biconditional p ↔ q is true precisely when:
o: both p and q are false
p and q have different truth values
p and q have the same truth value
at least one of p or q is true
questions.e: A biconditional is true exactly when both components share the same truth value (both true or both false).

questions.q: 'A necessary condition for the Cubs to win the World Series is that they sign a right-handed relief pitcher.' Restated as a conditional, this is:
o: If the Cubs win the World Series, then they sign a right-handed relief pitcher
If the Cubs sign a right-handed relief pitcher, then they win the World Series
The Cubs win the World Series and sign a right-handed relief pitcher
If the Cubs do not sign a pitcher, then they win the World Series
questions.e: A necessary condition q for p is expressed as p → q: if the Cubs win (p), then they must have signed the pitcher (q).

questions.q: 'A sufficient condition for Ralph to visit California is that he goes to Disneyland.' Restated as a conditional, this is:
o: Ralph goes to Disneyland and visits California
If Ralph goes to Disneyland, then he visits California
If Ralph does not go to Disneyland, then he does not visit California
If Ralph visits California, then he goes to Disneyland
questions.e: A sufficient condition p for q is expressed p → q: going to Disneyland (p) is enough to guarantee visiting California (q).

questions.q: The phrase 'p only if q' translates into which conditional?
questions.e: 'p only if q' means p → q. For example, 'John takes calculus only if he has senior standing' becomes 'if John takes calculus, then he has senior standing'.

questions.q: Given p = true, q = false, and r = true, what is the truth value of (p ∧ q) → r?
questions.e: (p ∧ q) = (T ∧ F) = F. A conditional with a false hypothesis is always true, so F → T = true.

questions.q: Given p = true, q = false, and r = true, what is the truth value of p ∧ (q → r)?
questions.e: (q → r) = (F → T) = T (false hypothesis makes a conditional true). Then p ∧ T = T ∧ T = true.

questions.q: Let p: '1 > 2' (false) and q: '3 < 6' (true). Considering p → q and its converse q → p, which statement is correct?
o: Both p → q and q → p are true
Both p → q and q → p are false
p → q is true but its converse q → p is false
p → q is false but its converse q → p is true
questions.e: p → q has a false hypothesis, so it is true. The converse q → p is 'true → false', which is false. A conditional can be true while its converse is false.

questions.q: A conditional proposition whose hypothesis is false is always:
questions.e: When the hypothesis is false, the conditional is vacuously true regardless of the conclusion (e.g. 'If 1 > 2, then 3 < 6' is true because 1 > 2 is false).

questions.q: The contrapositive of 'If 1 < 4, then 5 > 8' stated in words is:
o: If 5 is not greater than 8, then 1 is not less than 4
If 1 is not less than 4, then 5 is not greater than 8
If 1 < 4, then 5 is not greater than 8
questions.e: The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p, negating and swapping both parts: 'if 5 is not greater than 8, then 1 is not less than 4'.

questions.q: 'You can access the internet from campus only if you are a computer science major or you are not a freshman.' Using p: access the internet, q: computer science major, r: freshman, this is written:
questions.e: 'p only if X' means p → X, and 'q or not a freshman' is (q ∨ ¬r), giving p → (q ∨ ¬r).

questions.q: 'The message is scanned for viruses whenever the message was sent from an unknown system.' With p: the message is scanned for viruses and q: the message was sent from an unknown system, this is:
questions.e: 'A whenever B' means B → A. Here 'scanned (p) whenever sent from unknown system (q)' is q → p.

questions.q: Two compound propositions P and Q are logically equivalent (P ≡ Q) when:
o: One can be derived from the other by a single inference rule
They contain the same number of connectives
They are both true for at least one assignment of truth values
They have the same truth value for every combination of truth values of their component propositions
questions.e: P ≡ Q means that for any truth values of the constituent propositions, P and Q are either both true or both false.

questions.q: By De Morgan's law, ¬(p ∨ q) is logically equivalent to:
questions.e: De Morgan's law states (p ∨ q)' ≡ p' ∧ q': the negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations.

questions.q: By De Morgan's law, ¬(p ∧ q) is logically equivalent to:
questions.e: De Morgan's law states (p ∧ q)' ≡ p' ∨ q': the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations.

questions.q: The negation of the conditional p → q is logically equivalent to:
questions.e: ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q: the only way a conditional fails is when the hypothesis holds but the conclusion does not.

questions.q: The biconditional p ↔ q is logically equivalent to which conjunction of conditionals?
questions.e: p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p): the biconditional holds when both directions of implication hold.

questions.q: The process of drawing a conclusion from a sequence of propositions is called:
questions.e: Drawing a conclusion from a sequence of given propositions (hypotheses) is deductive reasoning.

questions.q: In an argument, the given propositions from which a conclusion is drawn are called:
questions.e: The given propositions are the hypotheses or premises; the proposition that follows from them is the conclusion.

questions.q: An argument is said to be valid when:
o: The hypotheses and conclusion are all false
The conclusion is true regardless of the hypotheses
At least one hypothesis is true
Whenever all the hypotheses are true, the conclusion must also be true
questions.e: An argument is valid if, whenever all hypotheses p1,...,pn are true, the conclusion q must also be true.

questions.q: An argument that is not valid is also called:
questions.e: An invalid argument is called a fallacy.

questions.q: Consider the true premises: 'The bug is in module 17 or in module 81', 'The bug is a numerical error', and 'Module 81 has no numerical error'. What is the valid conclusion?
o: The bug is in both modules
questions.e: Since the bug is a numerical error and module 81 has none, the bug cannot be in module 81; from 'module 17 or module 81' it must be in module 17.

questions.q: In the proof formula P · P = C, what does C represent?
questions.e: In the proof formula, each P is a premise and C is the conclusion that results from combining the premises.

questions.q: A set of premises (requirements) is said to be consistent when:
o: They are all false at the same time
Exactly one of them is true
There is an assignment of truth values making all of them true simultaneously
questions.e: For requirements to be consistent, all of them can be true at once with no contradiction.

questions.q: Consider the requirements: p ∨ q, ¬p, and p → q. Are these consistent?
o: No — they always contradict each other
No — because p → q is a fallacy
Yes — only when both p and q are true
Yes — taking p false and q true makes all three true
questions.e: With p = false: ¬p is true, p ∨ q needs q true (F ∨ T = T), and p → q is F → T = T. All three hold, so they are consistent.

questions.q: From the premises 'p → q' and 'q', concluding 'p' is:
questions.e: Affirming the consequent (p → q, q, therefore p) is a fallacy; a truth table shows the conclusion can be false while the premises are true.

questions.q: Every deductive argument can be written in which general form?
o: If p1 and p2 and ... and pn, then q
Not (p1 and p2 and ... and pn)
p1 if and only if q
p1 or p2 or ... or pn
questions.e: Any argument has the form: if p1 and p2 and ... and pn (the hypotheses) are all true, then q (the conclusion).

questions.q: To show that ¬(p → q) is logically equivalent to p ∧ ¬q, one demonstrates that:
o: They contain the same propositional variables
The two expressions have identical columns in a truth table
One implies the other but not conversely
questions.e: Logical equivalence is established by showing the two compound propositions have the same truth value in every row of a truth table.

questions.q: In writing arguments, the symbol ∴ means:
questions.e: The symbol ∴ is read 'therefore' and precedes the consequent (conclusion) of an argument.

questions.q: The rule of modus ponens is also known as:
o: The law of the excluded middle
questions.e: Modus ponens (from p and p → q infer q) is also called the law of detachment.

questions.q: Modus ponens allows you to infer which conclusion from the premises p and p → q?
questions.e: Modus ponens: given p and p → q, conclude q.

questions.q: Modus tollens allows you to infer which conclusion from the premises p → q and ¬q?
questions.e: Modus tollens: given p → q and ¬q, conclude ¬p.

questions.q: Which rule of inference is described as 'the mode of affirming'?
questions.e: Modus ponens is 'the mode of affirming' (it affirms the hypothesis to detach the conclusion).

questions.q: Which rule of inference is described as 'the mode of denying'?
questions.e: Modus tollens is 'the mode of denying' (it denies the conclusion to reject the hypothesis).

questions.q: The rule of addition permits inferring which conclusion from the single premise p?
questions.e: Addition: from p, infer p ∨ q (any disjunction containing p follows from p).

questions.q: The rule of simplification permits inferring which conclusion from the premise p ∧ q?
questions.e: Simplification: from p ∧ q, infer p (either conjunct follows from a conjunction).

questions.q: The rule of conjunction permits inferring which conclusion from the two premises p and q?
questions.e: Conjunction: from p and q separately, infer p ∧ q.

questions.q: The rule of hypothetical syllogism permits inferring which conclusion from p → q and q → r?
questions.e: Hypothetical syllogism chains two conditionals: from p → q and q → r, infer p → r.

questions.q: The rule of disjunctive syllogism permits inferring which conclusion from p ∨ q and ¬p?
questions.e: Disjunctive syllogism: from p ∨ q and ¬p, infer q (if one disjunct is false, the other must hold).

questions.q: The rule of resolution permits inferring which conclusion from p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r?
questions.e: Resolution: from p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r, infer q ∨ r.

questions.q: 'It is below freezing now. Therefore, it is either below freezing or raining now.' Which rule of inference is used?
questions.e: From p ('it is below freezing') the argument concludes p ∨ q ('below freezing or raining'), which is the addition rule.

questions.q: 'It is below freezing and raining now. Therefore, it is below freezing now.' Which rule of inference is used?
questions.e: From p ∧ q ('below freezing and raining') the argument concludes p ('below freezing'), which is the simplification rule.

questions.q: 'If it rains today, then we will not have a barbecue today. If we do not have a barbecue today, then we will have a barbecue tomorrow. Therefore, if it rains today, then we will have a barbecue tomorrow.' Which rule is used?
questions.e: The argument chains p → ¬q and ¬q → r to conclude p → r, which is hypothetical syllogism.

questions.q: An inference rule is best described as:
o: A rule for combining sets into a union
A statement that is always false
A method for negating a proposition
A pattern guaranteeing that if certain antecedent statements are all true, a related consequent statement is true
questions.e: An inference rule is a pattern establishing that if a set of antecedent statements of certain forms are all true, then a related consequent statement can be validly deduced as true.

questions.q: A proof by mathematical induction consists of which two steps?
o: A basis step and a contradiction step
A union step and an intersection step
A basis step and an inductive step
A hypothesis step and a conclusion step
questions.e: Mathematical induction requires a basis step (verify P(1)) and an inductive step (show P(k) implies P(k+1)).

questions.q: For a statement P(n) about positive integers, the basis step typically establishes that:
o: P(n) is false for some n
questions.e: The basis step verifies the statement for the smallest value, showing P(1) is true.

questions.q: In the inductive step of a proof by induction, one assumes P(k) is true and then shows that:
questions.e: The inductive step proves the implication P(k) → P(k+1): assuming the statement for k, establish it for k+1.

questions.q: If P(1) is true and the truth of P(k) implies the truth of P(k+1) for every positive integer k, then by mathematical induction:
o: P(n) is true for all natural numbers n
P(n) is true only for n = 1
P(n) is true only for even n
questions.e: The two conditions together imply that P(n) holds for all natural numbers n.

questions.q: The formula proven by induction for the sum of the first n positive integers, 1 + 2 + ... + n, is:
questions.e: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, a standard result proved by mathematical induction.

questions.q: The formula proven by induction for the sum of the first n odd positive integers, 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n-1), is:
Using the formula n(n+1)/2, what is the value of 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 10?
Using the formula n^2 for the sum of the first n odd numbers, what is 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9?
questions.e: There are 5 odd terms, so the sum is 5^2 = 25.

questions.q: The 'falling dominoes/tiles' analogy for mathematical induction captures which idea?
o: Only the first and last tiles fall
The first tile falls (basis), and any falling tile knocks over its successor (inductive step), so all tiles fall
Tiles fall only if pushed individually
All tiles fall at exactly the same instant
questions.e: The first tile falling represents the basis step; each falling tile knocking over the next represents P(k) → P(k+1); together every tile falls, i.e. P(n) holds for all n.

questions.q: Which of the following is cited as a use of mathematical induction?
o: Proving the correctness of certain computer programs
questions.e: Mathematical induction is used to prove results about the complexity of algorithms, the correctness of certain programs, and theorems about graphs and trees.

questions.q: In proving 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n-1) = n^2 by induction, the basis step checks which equality?
questions.e: For n = 1, the single term is 2(1) - 1 = 1 and the right side is 1^2 = 1, so the basis step verifies 1 = 1^2.

questions.q: In the inductive step for proving 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, what is added to both sides of the assumed equality for k to obtain the case k+1?
questions.e: Starting from 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2, adding (k+1) to both sides yields the sum up to (k+1), which simplifies to (k+1)(k+2)/2.

questions.q: A set is best defined as:
o: A rule mapping inputs to outputs
A sequence in which order matters
A collection of objects called its elements
questions.e: A set is a collection of objects; these objects are called the elements (or members) of the set.

questions.q: An object belonging to a set is also called a:
questions.e: An element of a set is also called a member of that set.

questions.q: A set that contains no elements is called the empty set. Which of these is another name for it?
questions.e: The empty set (containing no elements) is also called the null set or void set.

questions.q: Which notation correctly denotes the empty set?
questions.e: The empty set is written as { } or with the symbol ∅.

questions.q: In set notation, {paper, scissors, rock, rock} is the same set as {paper, scissors, rock} because:
o: Every set must contain the empty set as an element
questions.e: In a set, duplicates are not counted, so repeating 'rock' does not create a different set.

questions.q: Which statement about the order of elements in a set is correct?
o: Sets must be listed in alphabetical order
Only the first listed element counts
Order is irrelevant, so {paper, scissors, rock} and {rock, scissors, paper} are equal
Order matters, so those two are different sets
questions.e: The order of members in a set is irrelevant; the same elements in any order form equal sets.

questions.q: For the set A = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, the cardinality |A| is:
questions.e: |A| counts the elements; A has five members, so |A| = 5.

questions.q: The notation A ⊆ B means:
o: A is an element of B
Every member of A is also a member of B
A has more elements than B
A and B have no common elements
questions.e: A ⊆ B (A is a subset of B) means all members of A are also members of B.

questions.q: Which statement about subsets is always true?
o: The empty set is a subset of no set
A set can only be a subset of a larger set
No set is a subset of itself
Every set is a subset of itself
questions.e: A set is always a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set.

questions.q: The empty set is a subset of:
questions.e: The empty set is a subset of every set.

questions.q: The notation x ∈ S expresses which relationship?
o: x is an element (member) of the set S
S is a subset of x
x is a subset of S
questions.e: x ∈ S means x is an element of S (set membership), which is not the same as set inclusion (subset).

questions.q: The intersection A ∩ B is the set of all elements that are:
o: Neither in A nor in B
In A but not in B
questions.e: The intersection A ∩ B consists of the elements common to both A and B.

questions.q: Two sets S and T are called disjoint when:
questions.e: Sets are disjoint when their intersection is empty (they have no common element).

questions.q: The union A ∪ B is the set of all elements that are:
o: In A but not in B
In A or in B (or both)
questions.e: The union A ∪ B consists of all elements that are in A, in B, or in both.

questions.q: The set subtraction A − B (relative complement) consists of the elements that are:
o: In B but not in A
In A but not in B
questions.e: A − B, the relative complement, is the set of elements in A but not in B.

questions.q: The power set of a set A is:
o: The Cartesian product of A with itself
The set with only one element
The set of all subsets of A
questions.e: The power set of A is the set of all subsets of A.

questions.q: A singleton set is a set that:
o: Contains all subsets of another set
Is equal to the universal set
questions.e: A singleton set is a set with only one element.

questions.q: The complement of a set A (with respect to universal set U) is given by:
questions.e: The complement of A is U − A, all elements of the universal set not in A.

questions.q: Two sets are called overlapping when they:
o: Have at least one element in common
questions.e: Overlapping sets have elements in common; disjoint sets have no common element.

questions.q: The ordered pair (a, b) is considered equal to (b, a) only when:
o: a and b are both nonzero
questions.e: An ordered pair (a, b) is distinct from (b, a) unless a = b.

questions.q: The Cartesian product X × Y is defined as:
o: The union of X and Y
The set of all ordered pairs (x, y) with x ∈ X and y ∈ Y
The set of subsets of X
The set of elements common to X and Y
questions.e: X × Y is the set of all ordered pairs (x, y) where x comes from X and y comes from Y.

questions.q: If |X| = 3 and |Y| = 2, then the number of elements in X × Y is:
questions.e: The Cartesian product has |X| × |Y| = 3 × 2 = 6 ordered pairs.

questions.q: A restaurant serves 4 different appetizers and 3 different entrees. How many distinct (appetizer, entree) dinner combinations are possible?
questions.e: Each appetizer pairs with each entree, giving 4 × 3 = 12 combinations (the size of the Cartesian product).

questions.q: With A = {1, 6, 8} and B = {1, 3, 5, 7}, what is A ∩ B?
questions.e: The only element common to A and B is 1, so A ∩ B = {1}.

questions.q: With A = {1, 6, 8} and C = {3, 5, 7}, what is A ∩ C?
questions.e: A and C share no elements, so A ∩ C is empty and the sets are disjoint.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram, the universal set U is represented by:
questions.e: A Venn diagram represents the universal set U by a rectangle.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram, sets contained within the universal set are usually represented by:
questions.e: Sets within the universal set are usually drawn as circles inside the rectangle representing U.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram, two sets drawn so that their circles do not overlap represent:
questions.e: Circles with no region in common depict disjoint sets, which have no elements in common.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram, two sets whose circles share a common region represent:
questions.e: Overlapping circles indicate sets that share elements (overlapping sets).

questions.q: A Venn diagram in which one circle is drawn entirely inside another depicts:
questions.e: One circle drawn fully within another shows that the inner set is a subset of the outer set.

questions.q: Among 165 students: 8 take calculus, psychology and computer science; 33 take calculus and computer science; 20 take calculus and psychology; 24 take psychology and computer science; 79 take calculus; 83 take psychology; and 63 take computer science. Using inclusion-exclusion, how many take at least one of the three subjects?
questions.e: By inclusion-exclusion: 79 + 83 + 63 - 33 - 20 - 24 + 8 = 225 - 77 + 8 = 156 students take at least one subject.

questions.q: Among 165 students with the counts: 8 taking all three subjects, 33 calculus and computer science, 20 calculus and psychology, 24 psychology and computer science, 79 calculus, 83 psychology, 63 computer science — how many take NONE of the three subjects?
questions.e: At least one subject: 79 + 83 + 63 - 33 - 20 - 24 + 8 = 156. Then none = 165 - 156 = 9.

questions.q: To find the number of elements in a union of three sets from a Venn diagram, the inclusion-exclusion principle requires that you:
o: Add all the individual and intersection counts together
Subtract the triple intersection from each set size
Add the individual set sizes, subtract the pairwise intersections, then add back the triple intersection
Multiply the three set sizes together

An unordered collection of distinct objects
A rule that maps every input to a unique output

In sequences, only finitely many terms are permitted

The first element of the sequence

The sum of the terms of s

The reverse of the sequence s

questions.q: In sigma notation, the Greek letter Σ indicates:

A product of terms of a sequence

questions.q: In pi notation, the Greek letter Π indicates:

A product of terms of a sequence

questions.q: A string over a nonempty set X is defined as:
o: A finite sequence of elements from X
questions.e: A string over X is a finite sequence of elements drawn from X.

questions.q: The length |α| of a string α is:

The number of subsets of the string
The number of elements in the string
questions.e: The length of a string is the number of elements it contains; for example, b^2ac^3 has length 6.

questions.q: For a set X, the notation X* denotes:

The set of all non-null strings over X
The set of all strings over X, including the null string
questions.e: X* is the set of all strings over X including the null string λ.

questions.q: For a set X, the notation X+ denotes:

X* together with the null string
The set of even-length strings over X
The set of all subsets of X

questions.e: The strings of length 2 over {0,1} are 00, 01, 10, 11 — four strings.

questions.q: In strings, is the order of elements significant (for example, is b^2ac^3 equal to ac^3b^2)?
o: Order matters only for the null string
No, order is irrelevant, so they are equal
Yes, order matters, so b^2ac^3 ≠ ac^3b^2
They are equal only if lengths differ
questions.e: Order matters in strings, so b^2ac^3 and ac^3b^2 are different strings even though they use the same symbols.

questions.q: A binary relation R from a set X to a set Y is formally defined as:
o: A function from X onto Y
A subset of the Cartesian product X × Y
questions.e: A binary relation R from X to Y is a subset of X × Y; if (x, y) ∈ R we write x R y.

questions.q: When a relation R is defined from a set X to the same set X, it is called:
questions.e: If X = Y, the relation R is called a (binary) relation on X.

questions.q: The domain of a relation is:
o: The set of all first elements (x-values) of its ordered pairs
The set of all second elements (y-values)
The intersection of the two sets involved
The set of all pairs in the relation
questions.e: The domain is the set of all first components (x-values) of the ordered pairs in the relation.

questions.q: The range of a relation is:
o: The Cartesian product of the two sets
The set of all first elements (x-values)
The set of all second elements (y-values) of its ordered pairs
questions.e: The range is the set of all second components (y-values) of the ordered pairs.

questions.q: For the relation {(0, 1), (3, 22), (90, 34)}, the domain is:
questions.e: The domain collects the first elements of each pair: 0, 3, and 90.

questions.q: For the relation {(0, 1), (3, 22), (90, 34)}, the range is:
questions.e: The range collects the second elements of each pair: 1, 22, and 34.

questions.q: A relation R on a set A is reflexive if:
o: R is a subset of A
(a, a) ∈ R for every element a ∈ A
R contains no pairs of the form (a, a)
questions.e: R is reflexive when every element is related to itself: (a, a) ∈ R for all a ∈ A.

questions.q: A relation R on a set A is symmetric if:
o: R contains exactly one ordered pair
(a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R imply (a, c) ∈ R
questions.e: R is symmetric when, for all a and b, (a, b) ∈ R implies (b, a) ∈ R.

questions.q: In the digraph of a relation, an ordered pair of the form (x, x) corresponds to:
o: An isolated vertex with no edges
A loop (a directed edge from x to x)
questions.e: A pair (x, x) is drawn as a loop — a directed edge from a vertex back to itself.

questions.q: In the digraph of a relation, a pair (x, y) with x ≠ y is drawn as:
o: Two separate vertices with no edge
A directed edge (arrow) from x to y
questions.e: When (x, y) is in the relation and x ≠ y, an arrow (directed edge) is drawn from x to y.

questions.q: In the matrix of a relation R from X to Y, the entry in row x and column y is set to 1 when:
o: x is not related to y
x and y are in different sets
x R y (x is related to y)
questions.e: The matrix entry is 1 if x R y and 0 otherwise.

questions.q: Let X = {2, 3, 4} and Y = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Define R by (x, y) ∈ R if x divides y. Which is R?
For the divides relation on X = {2, 3, 4} to Y = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7} above, the range is:
questions.e: The second elements of the pairs (2,4),(2,6),(3,3),(3,6),(4,4) are 4, 6, 3, giving range {3, 4, 6}.

questions.q: A relation can be pictured by drawing dots for the elements and arrows for related pairs. This picture is called:
questions.e: A relation on a set is pictured with a digraph: vertices (dots) for elements and directed edges (arrows) for the pairs in the relation.

questions.q: A function f from X to Y is a relation from X to Y such that:
o: It contains at least one pair of the form (x, x)
Its domain is all of X and no x is paired with two different y-values
Every element of Y is used at least once
questions.e: For f: X → Y, we need Dom(f) = X and, if (x, y) and (x, y') are in f, then y = y' (each input has exactly one output).

questions.q: In the definition of a function, the requirement that 'the domain will never repeat' means:
o: No output value may be reused
Every output is associated with exactly one input
Each input element is associated with exactly one output
questions.e: It means no input is mapped to two different outputs; each x has a single image, though different x's may share an output.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required for a relation f from X to Y to be a function?
o: Every element of Y is the image of some element of X
No element of X maps to two different elements of Y
Each element of X maps to exactly one element of Y
The domain of f equals X
questions.e: That every element of Y is used describes an onto (surjective) function, which is not required for a relation merely to be a function.

questions.q: A pictorial representation of a function using arrows from inputs to outputs is called:
questions.e: An arrow diagram is a pictorial representation of a function.

questions.q: A function f is one-to-one (injective) if and only if:
o: it maps two distinct elements to the same value
every element of the codomain is an image
questions.e: A one-to-one function never maps two distinct elements to the same output: f(x) = f(y) forces x = y.

questions.q: A function f: A → B is onto (surjective) if and only if:
o: for every b ∈ B there is some a ∈ A with f(a) = b
distinct inputs always give distinct outputs
it has an inverse that is also a function
A and B have the same number of elements
questions.e: An onto function covers all of B: every element of the codomain is the image of at least one element of A.

questions.q: A bijection (one-to-one correspondence) is a function that is:
questions.e: A bijection is a function that is simultaneously injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto).

questions.q: A function has an inverse function if and only if it is:
questions.e: An inverse exists exactly when the function is a bijection; only bijections are invertible.

questions.q: For the composition (f ∘ g)(a), which function is applied first?

questions.q: The composition (f ∘ g)(a) is defined as:

questions.q: The floor function, floor(x), is defined as:
o: The largest integer y such that y ≤ x
x rounded up to the next integer
The smallest integer y such that y ≥ x
questions.e: The floor of x is the largest integer not exceeding x.

questions.q: The ceiling function, ceiling(x), is defined as:
o: x rounded to the nearest even integer
The largest integer y such that y ≤ x
The integer part of x with the fraction dropped
The smallest integer y such that y ≥ x
questions.e: The ceiling of x is the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to x.

questions.q: What is the value of floor(-0.5)?
questions.e: The floor is the largest integer ≤ -0.5, which is -1.

questions.q: What is the value of ceiling(-0.5)?
questions.e: The ceiling is the smallest integer ≥ -0.5, which is 0.

questions.q: What is the value of floor(8.3)?
questions.e: The largest integer not exceeding 8.3 is 8.

questions.q: What is the value of ceiling(9.1)?
questions.e: The smallest integer greater than or equal to 9.1 is 10.

questions.q: For positive numbers a and n, the expression a mod n gives:
o: The product of a and n
The remainder when a is divided by n
The quotient when a is divided by n
questions.e: The modulo operation a mod n returns the remainder after dividing a by n.

questions.e: Since 8 is less than 12, dividing 8 by 12 leaves a remainder of 8.

questions.e: 199673 is odd, so dividing by 2 leaves a remainder of 1.

As s mod 10, where s is the simple sum of all digits
As the number of dashes in the code

questions.q: For the ISBN whose first nine digits are 0 8 0 6 5 0 9 5 9, the weighted sum is s = 249. What is the check character (s mod 11)?
questions.e: 249 mod 11 = 7 (since 11 × 22 = 242 and 249 - 242 = 7), so the check character is 7.

questions.e: 132 mod 11 = 0 (since 11 × 12 = 132), so 132 is stored in cell 0.

questions.q: Using the hash function h(n) = n mod 11, which cell does the value 257 map to?
questions.e: 257 mod 11 = 4 (since 11 × 23 = 253 and 257 - 253 = 4), so 257 maps to cell 4.

questions.q: A simple graph is a graph that contains:
o: No loops and no multiple (parallel) edges
questions.e: A simple graph has neither loops nor multiple edges between the same pair of vertices.

questions.q: A graph that may contain multiple (parallel) edges between the same pair of vertices is called:
questions.e: A multigraph permits multiple edges joining the same pair of vertices.

questions.q: A pseudograph is a graph that may contain:
o: Loops (edges from a vertex to itself)
questions.e: A pseudograph is the most general undirected type and may contain loops as well as multiple edges.

questions.q: An acquaintanceship graph is characterized by having:
o: No loops and no parallel edges
questions.e: An acquaintanceship graph has no loops and no parallel edges (a person is not their own acquaintance, and two people are either acquainted or not).

questions.q: An influence graph is best described as:
o: A directed graph with no loops
A graph with parallel edges only
questions.e: An influence graph is a directed graph containing no loops (a person is not considered to influence themselves).

questions.q: In a precedence graph, each vertex represents:
o: A person in a social network
questions.e: In a precedence graph each vertex represents a statement of a computer program.

questions.q: In a precedence graph, an edge from statement a to statement b indicates that:
o: Statements a and b are identical
Statements a and b can be executed in any order
Statement b cannot be executed before statement a
Statement a must be executed after statement b
questions.e: An edge from a to b means b depends on a and cannot be executed before a has been executed.

questions.q: The purpose of a precedence graph is to model:
o: The dependence of statements so that some may be executed concurrently
The storage of keys in a hash table
The results of a sports tournament
questions.e: A precedence graph captures which statements depend on others, which is important when executing statements concurrently without violating dependencies.

questions.q: A round-robin tournament is one in which:
o: Each team plays every other team exactly once, with no ties allowed
Ties are decided by a coin toss
Each team plays only one other team
Teams may play each other multiple times
questions.e: In a round-robin tournament every team plays every other team exactly once and no ties are allowed.

questions.q: When a round-robin tournament is modeled by a directed graph, an edge (a, b) means:
o: Team a and team b did not play
questions.e: In the directed-graph model, the edge (a, b) is drawn when team a beats team b.

questions.q: The directed graph modeling a round-robin tournament is:
o: A simple directed graph with no loops or multiple directed edges
questions.e: Because no team plays another more than once and no team plays itself, the tournament graph is a simple directed graph with no loops or multiple directed edges.

questions.q: Which graph type is permitted to have loops that a simple graph forbids?
questions.e: A pseudograph may contain loops, whereas a simple graph forbids both loops and multiple edges.

questions.q: What distinguishes a multigraph from a simple graph?
o: A multigraph can have only one vertex
A multigraph allows multiple (parallel) edges between the same two vertices
questions.e: The key difference is that a multigraph permits parallel edges between a pair of vertices, which a simple graph does not.

questions.q: Which of the following graphs is directed?
o: A simple graph of city connections
questions.e: An influence graph is directed (influence goes one way), whereas an acquaintanceship graph is undirected.

questions.q: A tree is formally defined as:
o: A graph in which every pair of vertices is joined by an edge
A connected undirected graph with no simple circuits
A directed graph in which every vertex has a loop
Any graph that contains at least one cycle
questions.e: A tree is a connected undirected graph that contains no simple circuits (cycles).

questions.q: If one vertex of a graph cannot be reached from the others, the graph:
o: Is not a tree, because a tree must be connected
Is still a tree, as long as it has no cycles
questions.e: A tree must be connected; if some vertex is unreachable, the graph is disconnected and therefore not a tree.

questions.q: A rooted tree is formed from a tree by:
o: Adding a loop at every vertex
Choosing one vertex as the root and directing every edge away from it
questions.e: To make a rooted tree, one vertex is designated as the root and each edge is directed away from the root.

questions.q: In a rooted tree, a vertex that has no children is called:
questions.e: A vertex with no children is a leaf; a vertex that has children is an internal vertex.

questions.q: In a rooted tree, a vertex that has at least one child is called:
questions.e: A vertex that has children is called an internal vertex.

questions.q: In a rooted tree, two vertices that share the same parent are called:
questions.e: Sibling vertices are those that have the same parent.

questions.q: The level of the root of a rooted tree is:
questions.e: The root is at level 0; its children are at level 1, and so on.

questions.q: The level of a vertex v in a rooted tree is defined as:
o: The length of the unique path from the root to v
The total number of vertices in the tree
The number of leaves below v
The number of children v has
questions.e: The level of v is the length of the unique path from the root to v.

questions.q: The height of a rooted tree is defined as:
o: The number of leaves in the tree
The number of edges leaving the root
The maximum of the levels of its vertices
questions.e: The height of a rooted tree is the largest level occurring among all its vertices.

questions.q: The ancestors of a non-root vertex v are:
o: All the vertices on the path from the root to v
All the vertices at the same level as v
questions.e: The ancestors of a non-root vertex are all vertices lying on the path from the root down to that vertex.

questions.q: The descendants of a vertex v are:
o: Only the immediate children of v
All the leaves of the tree
All the vertices on the path from the root to v
All the vertices that have v as an ancestor
questions.e: The descendants of v are all vertices that have v as one of their ancestors.

questions.q: A rooted tree is called an m-ary tree if:
o: The tree has exactly m leaves
Every internal vertex has exactly m children
Every internal vertex has no more than m children
questions.e: An m-ary tree is a rooted tree in which every internal vertex has at most m children.

questions.q: A rooted tree is called a full m-ary tree if:
o: It has exactly m internal vertices
Every leaf is at the same level
Every internal vertex has at most m children
Every internal vertex has exactly m children
questions.e: In a full m-ary tree, every internal vertex has exactly m children (not merely at most m).

questions.q: A binary tree is a rooted tree in which:
o: Every internal vertex has exactly 3 children
Every internal vertex has no more than 2 children
questions.e: A binary tree is a rooted tree where every internal vertex has at most 2 children; a full binary tree has exactly 2 per internal vertex.

questions.q: In an ordered binary tree, the two possible children of a vertex are distinguished as:
o: The first and the last ancestor
The root child and the leaf child
The left child and the right child
The upper child and the lower child
questions.e: An ordered binary tree orders the children of each vertex; the two possible children are called the left child and the right child.

questions.q: An ordered rooted tree is a rooted tree in which:
o: The children of each internal vertex are ordered
Every internal vertex has exactly one child
questions.e: In an ordered rooted tree, the children of each internal vertex are assigned a specific order.

questions.q: A rooted tree that is drawn with a specified root, from which every edge points away, is best described as:
questions.e: Once a root is chosen and edges are directed away from it, the structure is a rooted tree; without a designated root it is an unrooted tree.

questions.q: A rooted binary tree of height H is called balanced if:
o: Every internal vertex has exactly two children
All of its leaves are at level H only
All of its leaves are at levels H or H-1
questions.e: A binary tree of height H is balanced when all its leaves lie at level H or level H-1.

questions.q: In a binary search tree, the key value of each vertex is:
o: Equal to the keys in both subtrees
Less than every key in its left subtree and greater than every key in its right subtree
Greater than every key in its left subtree and less than every key in its right subtree
Unrelated to the keys in its subtrees
questions.e: In a BST, each vertex's key is greater than all keys in its left subtree and less than all keys in its right subtree.

questions.q: Which is a required property of the keys stored in a binary search tree?
o: All vertices contain the same key value
Each vertex contains a distinct key value that can be compared with 'greater than' and 'less than'
questions.e: A BST requires each vertex to hold a distinct key value, and the keys must be comparable using 'greater than' and 'less than'.

questions.q: The shape of a binary search tree depends on:
o: Nothing; all BSTs have the same shape
The height of the alphabet used
Only the number of keys, not their order
Its key values and their order of insertion
questions.e: The BST's shape is determined by the key values and the order in which they are inserted.

questions.q: When building a binary search tree, the first value inserted becomes:
o: The right child of an empty node
A leaf at the deepest level
questions.e: The first value inserted is placed at the root of the binary search tree.

questions.q: When inserting a new value into a binary search tree, at each vertex you move left if the new value is:
o: Equal to the value at the current vertex
Less than the value at the current vertex
Greater than the value at the current vertex
questions.e: Each new value is compared with the current vertex, moving left if it is smaller and right if it is larger, until it becomes a new leaf.

questions.q: Inserting the letters J, E, F, T, A into an initially empty binary search tree in that order places which letter at the root?
questions.e: The first value inserted becomes the root, so J is the root.

questions.q: Inserting J, E, F, T, A in order into a binary search tree, where does T end up?
o: As the right child of the root J
As the left child of the root J
questions.e: T is greater than the root J, so it moves right and, finding no right child, becomes the right child of J.

questions.q: A procedure for systematically visiting every vertex of an ordered binary tree is called:
questions.e: A tree traversal is a procedure that systematically visits every vertex of an ordered binary tree; the three named traversals are preorder, inorder, and postorder.

questions.q: The three standard tree traversals of an ordered binary tree are:
questions.e: The three named traversals are preorder, inorder, and postorder; each is defined recursively.

questions.q: In a preorder traversal of an ordered binary tree, the order of steps is:
o: Traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the root
Traverse the left subtree, then visit the root, then the right subtree
Visit the root, then the right subtree, then the left subtree
Visit the root, then traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree
questions.e: Preorder: visit the root first, then traverse the left subtree in preorder, then the right subtree in preorder.

questions.q: In an inorder traversal of an ordered binary tree, the order of steps is:
o: Traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the root
Visit the root, then the right subtree, then the left subtree
Traverse the left subtree, then visit the root, then traverse the right subtree
Visit the root, then the left subtree, then the right subtree
questions.e: Inorder: traverse the left subtree in inorder, then visit the root, then traverse the right subtree in inorder.

questions.q: In a postorder traversal of an ordered binary tree, the order of steps is:
o: Traverse the left subtree, then visit the root, then the right subtree
Visit the root, then the right subtree, then the left subtree
Traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the root
Visit the root, then the left subtree, then the right subtree
questions.e: Postorder: traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then end by visiting the root.

questions.q: Tree traversals of an ordered binary tree are defined:
questions.e: The preorder, inorder, and postorder traversals are all defined recursively.

questions.q: The main advantage of storing ordered items in a binary search tree is that it enables:
o: Elimination of the need for a root
Efficient searching for any stored item
questions.e: A binary search tree stores items so that any stored item can be found efficiently when all items are ordered.

questions.q: In a binary expression tree, each leaf node contains:
questions.e: In a binary expression tree, each leaf holds a single operand and each nonleaf holds a single binary operator.

questions.q: In a binary expression tree, each nonleaf (internal) node contains:
questions.e: Each nonleaf node of a binary expression tree contains one binary operator, applied to the results of its two subtrees.

questions.q: An inorder traversal of a binary expression tree produces the expression in which notation?
questions.e: Inorder traversal yields infix notation; preorder yields prefix and postorder yields postfix.

questions.q: A preorder traversal of a binary expression tree produces the expression in which notation?
questions.e: Preorder traversal of an expression tree gives prefix (Polish) notation.

questions.q: A postorder traversal of a binary expression tree produces the expression in which notation?
questions.e: Postorder traversal of an expression tree gives postfix (reverse Polish) notation.

questions.q: For an expression tree with root '-' and children operands 8 and 5 (left to right), the postfix form and value are:
questions.e: Postorder gives 8 5 -, which evaluates as 8 - 5 = 3.

questions.q: Consider the expression written in infix as ((4 + 2) * 3). What is its value?
questions.e: Evaluating inside out: (4 + 2) = 6, then 6 * 3 = 18.

questions.q: The infix expression ((4 + 2) * 3) corresponds to which prefix expression?
questions.e: Preorder traversal of the tree (root *, left subtree +(4,2), right 3) gives * + 4 2 3.

questions.q: The infix expression ((4 + 2) * 3) corresponds to which postfix expression?
questions.e: Postorder traversal (left subtree, right subtree, root) gives 4 2 + 3 *.

questions.q: Evaluate the postfix expression 8 5 - 4 2 + 3 / *.
When a binary expression tree represents an expression, the level of an operator node indicates:
o: Nothing about the order of evaluation
Its relative precedence — operations higher in the tree are evaluated later, and the root's operation is last
The number of operands in the expression
That higher operators are always evaluated first
questions.e: Levels indicate precedence: operations at higher levels are performed later, and the operation at the root is always performed last.

questions.q: In the Universal Address System for an ordered rooted tree, the root is labeled:
questions.e: In the Universal Address System, the root is labeled 0, and its children are labeled 1, 2, ..., k from left to right.

questions.q: In the Universal Address System, if a vertex has label A, its children (left to right) are labeled:
questions.e: A vertex with label A has its children labeled A.1, A.2, ..., A.k from left to right.

questions.q: In an ordered rooted tree using the Universal Address System, a vertex has the address 3.4.5.2.4. At what level is this vertex?
questions.e: The number of components in the address equals the level; 3.4.5.2.4 has five parts, so the vertex is at level 5.

questions.q: A vertex in an ordered rooted tree has Universal Address 3.4.5.2.4. What is the address of its parent?
questions.e: The parent's address is obtained by dropping the last component, giving 3.4.5.2.

questions.q: A vertex in an ordered rooted tree has Universal Address 3.4.5.2.4. Counting the vertex itself, what is the least number of siblings it can have at that position?
questions.e: The final label 4 means there are at least four children (labeled .1, .2, .3, .4) among that parent's children, so there are at least 4 vertices including this one.

questions.q: The eccentricity of a vertex in an unrooted tree is defined as:
o: The number of children of that vertex
The length of the longest simple path beginning at that vertex
The number of leaves in the tree
The shortest path between two leaves
questions.e: The eccentricity of a vertex is the length of the longest simple path that begins at that vertex.

questions.q: A vertex of a tree is called a center if:
o: No vertex in the tree has a smaller eccentricity
It has the largest eccentricity of all vertices
questions.e: A center is a vertex whose eccentricity is minimal — no other vertex has a smaller eccentricity.

questions.q: If each of the 26 letters of the alphabet is encoded with a fixed-length bit string, the shortest length that suffices is:
questions.e: Five bits give 2^5 = 32 combinations, enough for 26 letters, whereas four bits give only 16.

questions.q: A prefix code is a coding scheme in which:
o: Each code word is a prefix of the next
No code word is a prefix of any other code word
The most frequent letter has the longest code
Every code word has the same length
questions.e: In a prefix code, no code is the prefix of any other, which lets a bit string be decoded unambiguously.

questions.q: When a prefix code is represented by a binary tree, the characters being encoded are placed at:
questions.e: In the binary-tree representation of a prefix code, the leaves represent the characters of the string.

questions.q: In the binary-tree representation of a prefix code, an edge leading to a left child is labeled 0 and an edge to a right child is labeled 1. The code for a character is:
o: The label of the root only
The sequence of edge labels on the path from the root to that character's leaf
The number of the level at which the leaf lies
questions.e: A character's code is the sequence of edge labels along the unique path from the root to the leaf holding that character.

questions.q: Using the prefix code e = 0, a = 10, t = 110, n = 1110, s = 1111, decode the bit string 11111011100.
questions.e: Reading a prefix code left to right: 1111 = s, 10 = a, 1110 = n, 0 = e, giving 'sane'.

questions.q: Huffman coding builds a variable-rate prefix code by using which property of the symbols?
o: The number of bits in their ASCII codes
The length of the message only
questions.e: Huffman coding uses the frequencies of symbols to build a variable-rate prefix code.

questions.q: In a Huffman code, symbols that occur more frequently are assigned:
questions.e: Huffman coding assigns shorter codes to more frequent symbols and longer codes to rarer symbols, reducing the total number of bits.

questions.q: Huffman coding is named after David A. Huffman, who introduced it in:
questions.e: Huffman coding was introduced by David A. Huffman in 1951.

questions.q: When a Huffman tree is built for a text, the frequency stored at the root of the completed tree equals:
o: The total number of characters in the text
The length of the longest code word
The number of distinct characters in the text
questions.e: The root's frequency equals the sum of all character frequencies, i.e. the total number of characters in the text.

questions.q: Why does a message encoded with a Huffman (prefix) code need no separator character between code words?
o: Because no code word is a prefix of another, so the boundaries are unambiguous
Because the message is always short
Because separators are added automatically by the alphabet
Because every code word has the same length
questions.e: Since it is a prefix code (no code is a prefix of another), the decoder can always tell where one code word ends and the next begins, so no separator is needed.

questions.q: The essential idea that motivates variable-length encoding (as opposed to fixed 5-bit codes) is to:
o: Use fewer total bits by giving frequent letters shorter codes
Use more bits so the message is harder to read
Give every letter the same code
questions.e: Variable-length coding saves memory and transmission time by encoding frequently occurring letters with short bit strings and rare letters with longer ones.

questions.q: A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph is:
o: A directed version of the graph
A connected subgraph that contains no cycles
A subgraph that omits some of the vertices
Any subgraph that contains at least one cycle
questions.e: A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph is a connected subgraph, containing all the vertices, that has no cycles.

questions.q: If a connected graph G has n vertices, then any spanning tree of G has exactly:
questions.e: A spanning tree on n vertices always has exactly n - 1 edges.

questions.q: If a connected graph G has n vertices and m edges, the number of edges that must be deleted to obtain a spanning tree is:
questions.e: A spanning tree has n - 1 edges, so the number deleted is m - (n - 1) = m - n + 1.

questions.q: How many spanning trees can a single connected graph have?
o: It may have multiple (many) spanning trees
questions.e: A single connected graph may have multiple different spanning trees.

questions.q: In a graph, the term 'connected' means:
o: Every node is reachable from every other node
Every edge has an associated direction
questions.e: A graph is connected when every node can be reached from every other node.

questions.q: The cost (weight) of a spanning tree in a weighted graph is:
o: The cost of its most expensive edge
The sum of the costs of its edges
The cost of the cheapest edge only
questions.e: The cost of a spanning tree is the sum of the costs (weights) of the edges it contains.

questions.q: A minimum-cost spanning tree of a weighted connected undirected graph is:
o: Any subgraph with a cycle of minimum weight
A spanning tree whose total edge cost is the lowest possible
A spanning tree that uses the most edges
The single cheapest edge in the graph
questions.e: A minimum-cost spanning tree is a spanning tree of the graph with the lowest possible total edge cost.

questions.q: Prim's algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree by:
o: Starting at one node and repeatedly adding the cheapest edge to a node not yet in the tree
Deleting edges until no cycles remain
Adding edges in alphabetical order of their labels
Repeatedly adding the most expensive available edge
questions.e: Prim's algorithm starts from any one node and repeatedly adds the cheapest edge (and the node it leads to) whose node is not already in the spanning tree.

questions.q: In Prim's algorithm, an edge is rejected during a step if adding it would:
o: Create a cycle (connect two nodes already in the tree)
Add a new node to the tree
questions.e: Prim's algorithm avoids adding an edge between two nodes already in the tree, because that would form a cycle.

questions.q: To find any spanning tree (not necessarily minimum), one approach is to:
o: Connect every pair of vertices with an edge
Pick an initial node and, during a search, add each newly reached node together with the edge used to reach it
Add every edge of the graph to the tree
Delete all vertices of degree one
questions.e: Starting from an initial node and searching, each time a node not yet in the tree is found, both that node and the edge followed to reach it are added.

questions.q: The 'undirected' property required of a graph before finding a spanning tree means:
o: Its edges do not have an associated direction
Its edges each point one way
questions.e: Undirected means the edges have no associated direction, so they can be traversed either way.

questions.q: A weighted connected graph can have more than one minimum spanning tree when:
o: Different choices of equal-cost edges lead to trees of the same total minimum cost
Every edge has a distinct weight
questions.e: When ties occur among edge costs, alternative equal-weight choices can produce more than one spanning tree achieving the same minimum total cost.

questions.q: In formal language theory, a language is:
questions.e: A language is a set of strings; a grammar is a concise way to specify such a set.

questions.q: A grammar specifies a language by means of:
o: A list of every string in the language
questions.e: A grammar consists of a series of rewrite rules, each having a left-hand side and a right-hand side separated by an arrow.

questions.q: In a grammar rule, the arrow (→) is read as:
questions.e: The arrow → in a production rule is read 'may be replaced by'.

questions.q: Which of the following is a standard component of a context-free grammar?
questions.e: The parts of a context-free grammar are the alphabet, terminals, non-terminals, productions, and a start symbol.

questions.q: In a context-free grammar, non-terminal symbols are:
o: Symbols that may never be replaced
Symbols that may be replaced (further expanded)
questions.e: Non-terminal symbols are those that may be replaced or expanded further using the grammar's rules.

questions.q: In a context-free grammar, terminal symbols are:
o: Symbols that may not be replaced
Symbols that must be expanded further
questions.e: Terminal symbols are symbols that cannot be replaced; they are the final symbols appearing in generated strings.

questions.q: By the usual notational convention in these grammars, non-terminal symbols are written with:
questions.e: Non-terminal symbols are denoted by uppercase letters, while terminal symbols are denoted by lowercase letters.

questions.q: What makes a grammar rule 'context-free'? Every rule has the form A → P where:
o: A is a string of several terminals
P must be a single terminal
A is a single non-terminal, with no surrounding context
A appears on the right-hand side
questions.e: In a context-free rule A → P, the left-hand side A is a single non-terminal replaced regardless of any surrounding context — hence 'context-free'.

questions.q: In a context-free rule A → P, the right-hand side P may be:
o: Any sequence of terminals and non-terminals, and may even be empty (ε)
questions.e: P can be any sequence of terminals and non-terminals, and it may also be the empty string ε.

questions.q: The empty (null) string is denoted by which symbol and has what length?
questions.e: The empty or null string is denoted ε and contains no symbols, so its length is zero.

questions.q: The rule A → aA | ε is read as:
o: A may only be replaced by a
A must be replaced by both aA and ε simultaneously
A equals a times A plus epsilon
A may be replaced by aA or by the empty string
questions.e: The vertical bar separates alternatives, so A → aA | ε means A may be replaced by aA or by the empty string ε.

questions.q: For an alphabet V, the notation V* denotes:
o: The set of terminal symbols only
The set of all words (strings) over V
questions.e: V* denotes the set of all words (finite strings) over the alphabet V; a language over V is a subset of V*.

questions.q: An alphabet V, as used in defining a language, is:
o: A finite, nonempty set of symbols
questions.e: An alphabet V is a finite, nonempty set of elements called symbols.

questions.q: In the sample grammar S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b, every generated string contains:
o: At least one a followed by at least one b
Zero or more a's and no b's
Exactly one a and one b only
questions.e: With A → aA | a and B → bB | b, both A and B must produce at least one symbol, so every string has at least one a followed by at least one b (e.g. ab, aab, abb).

questions.q: To modify the grammar S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b so that it also generates the empty string and 'zero or more' a's and b's, you would:
o: Replace the base rules with A → aA | ε and B → bB | ε
questions.e: Allowing A → aA | ε and B → bB | ε lets A and B each generate the empty string, producing zero or more a's followed by zero or more b's.

questions.q: For the grammar with productions S → 11S and S → 0, the generated language L(G) is:
o: All strings that begin with an even number of 1s and end with a 0
questions.e: Each application of S → 11S adds two 1s, and S → 0 terminates the string; so L(G) = {0, 110, 11110, ...}: an even number of 1s followed by a 0.

questions.q: In Backus-Naur Form (BNF), the symbol used in place of the arrow → is:
questions.e: BNF uses ::= instead of →, encloses non-terminals in angle brackets < >, and groups productions with the same left side using |.

questions.q: In BNF notation, non-terminal symbols are written:
questions.e: BNF encloses non-terminal symbols within angle brackets, e.g. <integer>.

questions.q: In the Extended BNF notation, the postfix symbols * and + mean respectively:
questions.e: In Extended BNF, * means zero or more repetitions and + means one or more.

questions.q: A production rule in a context-free grammar must have on its left-hand side:
o: At least one non-terminal (a single non-terminal for CFG rules)
questions.e: Every production must have a non-terminal on its left-hand side; in a context-free grammar that left side is a single non-terminal.

questions.q: Finite state machines with no output are used to:
o: Determine whether an input string is accepted (recognized) or not
Generate an output string for every input
questions.e: An FSM with no output determines whether the input is accepted (recognized); an FSM with output instead generates output from the input.

questions.q: A finite state machine with output is used to:
o: Generate an output from the given input
Only decide acceptance of the input
Store keys in a hash table
questions.e: An FSM with output produces output from the given input, in contrast to an output-free FSM that only recognizes strings.

questions.q: Which two representations are commonly used to describe a finite state machine?
o: An adjacency matrix and a heap
A state diagram and a state transition table
A prefix code and a Huffman tree
A truth table and a Venn diagram
questions.e: A finite state machine is commonly represented by a state diagram or by a state transition table.

questions.q: A finite state machine with output is defined as the tuple M = (S, I, O, f, g, s0). In this definition, f is:
o: The transition function, f: S × I → S
questions.e: In M = (S, I, O, f, g, s0), f is the transition function mapping a (state, input) pair to a next state: f: S × I → S.

questions.q: In the finite-state machine with output M = (S, I, O, f, g, s0), the function g is:
o: The output function, g: S × I → O
questions.e: g is the output function, mapping a (state, input) pair to an output symbol: g: S × I → O.

questions.q: A finite-state automaton (a finite state machine with no output) is defined as M = (S, I, f, s0, F). The component F represents:
questions.e: In M = (S, I, f, s0, F), F is the set of final states (a subset of S), indicated by double circles in the state diagram.

questions.q: In the state diagram of a finite-state automaton, final (accepting) states are indicated by:
questions.e: Final states of a finite-state automaton are drawn as double circles.

questions.q: A string x is said to be recognized (accepted) by a finite-state automaton M = (S, I, f, s0, F) if:
o: f(s0, x) is a state in F
f(s0, x) is the initial state
x is longer than the number of states
questions.e: A string x is recognized when, starting from s0, it drives the machine to a final state — that is, f(s0, x) ∈ F.

questions.q: The language L(M) recognized by a finite-state automaton M is:
o: The set of all states of M
The set of all strings accepted by M
The set of transition functions of M
The output produced for a single input
questions.e: L(M) is the language recognized by M — the set of all strings that M accepts.

questions.q: A finite state machine with no output is also called a:
questions.e: A finite state machine with no output, having a set of final states, is called a finite-state automaton.

questions.q: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) over a binary alphabet can be designed, for example, to determine whether:
o: The graph has a spanning tree
The input contains an even number of 0s
The input is a valid English sentence
questions.e: A DFA over a binary alphabet can recognize, for instance, all strings containing an even number of 0s.

questions.q: Finite-state automata (FSMs with no output) are especially applied in:
o: Language recognition and the design and implementation of compilers
questions.e: FSMs with no output are used for language recognition and in the design and implementation of compilers.

questions.q: In cryptography, the original intelligible message is called the:
questions.e: The plaintext is the original intelligible message, before it is transformed.

questions.q: In cryptography, the transformed (coded) message is called the:
questions.e: The ciphertext is the transformed, coded form of the message.

questions.q: A cipher (cryptographic system) is:
o: An algorithm for transforming plaintext into ciphertext
questions.e: A cipher, or cryptographic system, is an algorithm for transforming plaintext into ciphertext.

questions.q: In cryptography, the key is:
o: Critical information used by the cipher, known only to the sender and receiver
The name of the encryption algorithm
questions.e: The key is critical information used by the cipher that is known only to the sender and receiver.

questions.q: The process of converting plaintext into ciphertext using a cipher and key is called:
questions.e: Encryption (enciphering) converts plaintext to ciphertext; decryption recovers the plaintext from the ciphertext.

questions.q: If encryption is written C = E(P, K), then decryption is written:
questions.e: Decryption recovers the plaintext from the ciphertext using the key: P = D(C, K).

questions.q: The Caesar cipher is a substitution cipher historically attributed to:
questions.e: The Caesar cipher is the earliest known substitution cipher, attributed to Julius Caesar.

questions.q: In the classic Caesar cipher, each letter of the message is replaced by the letter:
o: 3 places further down the alphabet, wrapping around from Z to A
At the mirror-image position in the alphabet
With the same position but uppercase
questions.e: In Caesar's cipher the key is 3: each character is replaced by the letter 3 places down, with the alphabet wrapping so that the letter after Z is A.

questions.q: The general Caesar cipher encryption of a letter p with shift key k is given by:
questions.e: The general Caesar cipher is C = E(k, p) = (p + k) mod 26, where k is the shift key.

questions.q: The decryption formula for the general Caesar cipher (shift key k) is:
questions.e: Decryption reverses the shift: p = D(k, C) = (C - k) mod 26.

questions.q: A brute-force attack on the basic Caesar cipher is easy because there are only:
questions.e: The Caesar cipher has only 25 possible non-trivial shift keys, so all can be tried until an intelligible message appears.

questions.q: The Caesar cipher can be broken even from a single known pair of (plaintext letter, ciphertext letter) because:
o: The key is written in the ciphertext
The difference between the two letters directly reveals the key
Every Caesar cipher uses no key
questions.e: With one matching plain/cipher letter pair, the key is simply the difference between them.

questions.q: Using the Caesar cipher C = (p + 3) mod 26 with A = 0, the plaintext letter M (p = 12) encrypts to:
questions.e: (12 + 3) mod 26 = 15, which corresponds to the letter P (with A = 0).

questions.q: Using the Caesar cipher C = (p + 3) mod 26 with A = 0, the plaintext word MEET encrypts to:
questions.e: M→P, E→H, E→H, T→W (each shifted 3 with wraparound), giving PHHW.

questions.q: Decrypting the Caesar ciphertext PHHW with key 3 using p = (C - 3) mod 26 gives the plaintext:
Using the affine cipher f(p) = (7p + 3) mod 26 with A = 0, the letter K (p = 10) encrypts to:
questions.e: f(10) = (7×10 + 3) mod 26 = 73 mod 26 = 21, which is the letter V.

questions.q: The more advanced affine encryption function has the general form:
questions.e: The affine cipher generalizes the Caesar shift to f(p) = (a·p + b) mod 26, using two parameters a and b.

questions.q: The branch of study concerned with the principles and methods of encryption is called:
questions.e: Cryptography is the study of encryption principles and methods; cryptanalysis is the study of breaking ciphers.
